# RxCostGuide — full index

Independent, clinician-reviewed guides to US prescription drug prices, copay cards, patient-assistance programs and Medicare coverage.
All prices approximate, US, verified against manufacturer savings pages and CMS.gov; retrieval date shown per page.
Reviewer: Dr. Faisal Irshad, MBBS, M.Phil Chemical Pathology (PMDC 54440-S).

## Dupixent (dupilumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/dupixent-cost/
Class: IL-4/IL-13 inhibitor biologic
Short answer: Dupixent costs about $3,800 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Dupixent MyWay copay card. Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap; uninsured patients can apply for free medication.

## Trelegy Ellipta (fluticasone/umeclidinium/vilanterol)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/trelegy-cost/
Class: Triple-therapy inhaler
Short answer: Trelegy costs about $650 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Trelegy copay card. Trelegy is in the second Medicare negotiation cycle, with a negotiated price effective 2027; until then Medicare patients use Part D and the $2,100 cap.

## Fasenra (benralizumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/fasenra-cost/
Class: IL-5 receptor biologic
Short answer: Fasenra costs about $5,000 per dose at list price (dosed every 8 weeks in maintenance). Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Fasenra copay card. Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Xolair (omalizumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/xolair-cost/
Class: Anti-IgE biologic
Short answer: Xolair costs roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month depending on your dose and weight. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Xolair Co-pay Card. Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Symbicort (budesonide/formoterol)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/symbicort-cost/
Class: ICS/LABA inhaler
Short answer: Branded Symbicort costs about $350 a month at list price, but a generic budesonide/formoterol is available and cheaper — often the best route. Commercially insured patients can also use the Symbicort savings card; uninsured patients should compare the generic with a discount card.

## Nucala (mepolizumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/nucala-cost/
Class: IL-5 antagonist (subcutaneous, every 4 weeks)
Short answer: Nucala's list price is ~$3,700 per dose (every 4 weeks), so few patients pay full price. With commercial insurance, the Nucala Co-pay Program can lower your cost to as little as $0 per prescription (annual maximum applies). On Medicare Part D, your out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026, and Together with GSK may help eligible patients who are uninsured or underinsured.

## Airsupra (albuterol/budesonide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/airsupra-cost/
Class: As-needed rescue inhaler (bronchodilator + inhaled steroid)
Short answer: Airsupra has a list price of ~$500 per inhaler. With commercial insurance, you may pay as little as $0 per inhaler with the Airsupra Savings Card (annual maximum applies). On Medicare Part D, the card can't be used, but your 2026 out-of-pocket spending on covered drugs is capped at $2,100, and the AZ&Me Prescription Savings Program may help if you qualify.

## Adbry (tralokinumab-ldrm)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/adbry-cost/
Class: IL-13 inhibitor (subcutaneous, every 2 weeks)
Short answer: Adbry has a list price of ~$2,000 per 2-syringe pack, so paying cash is expensive. With commercial insurance, you may pay as little as $0 per fill with the Adbry Copay Program. On Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but your total out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Spiriva (tiotropium)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/asthma-allergy-eczema/spiriva-cost/
Class: Long-acting anticholinergic bronchodilator (inhaler)
Short answer: Without insurance, Spiriva runs about ~$285–346/mo cash. With commercial insurance, the Spiriva Savings Card brings it to $35 per 30-day fill (not $0) for up to 12 fills/yr. On Medicare the card can't be used, but 2026 Part D out-of-pocket costs are capped at $2,100, and a generic tiotropium is available that may cost less.

## Humira (adalimumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/humira-cost/
Class: TNF inhibitor (biologic)
Short answer: Brand Humira lists around $7,000 a month (two pens). Since 2023 several adalimumab biosimilars (Amjevita, Cyltezo, Hyrimoz, Yuflyma, Simlandi and others) are available at far lower prices — some through low-cost channels for a few hundred dollars a month. Commercially insured patients can still reach $0 with the Humira Complete card; the biggest savings lever is the biosimilar.

## Skyrizi (risankizumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/skyrizi-cost/
Class: IL-23 inhibitor (biologic)
Short answer: Skyrizi lists around $21,000 per dose, but maintenance dosing is only every 8–12 weeks, so the annual figure (roughly $90,000+) matters more than any monthly number. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $5 per dose with the Skyrizi Complete card. There is no biosimilar. Medicare patients pay plan cost-share under the $2,100 cap.

## Stelara (ustekinumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/stelara-cost/
Class: IL-12/23 inhibitor (biologic)
Short answer: Brand Stelara lists around $25,000 per dose, dosed every 8–12 weeks in maintenance. Since 2025 ustekinumab biosimilars (Wezlana, Selarsdi, Pyzchiva and others) are available at lower prices. Commercially insured patients can reach $5 per dose with the Janssen withMe card; the biggest lever is now the biosimilar.

## Rinvoq (upadacitinib)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/rinvoq-cost/
Class: JAK inhibitor
Short answer: Rinvoq costs about $6,900 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $5 a month with the Rinvoq Complete copay card. Medicare patients pay plan cost-share up to the $2,100 Part D cap; uninsured patients can apply for free medication through AbbVie.

## Cosentyx (secukinumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/cosentyx-cost/
Class: IL-17A inhibitor
Short answer: Cosentyx costs several thousand dollars a month at list price (roughly $7,000/month-equivalent depending on dosing schedule). Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Cosentyx Connect copay card. Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Taltz (ixekizumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/taltz-cost/
Class: IL-17A inhibitor
Short answer: Taltz costs several thousand dollars a month at list price (roughly $7,000/month-equivalent depending on dosing). Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Taltz Together copay card. Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Enbrel (etanercept)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/enbrel-cost/
Class: TNF inhibitor
Short answer: Enbrel costs about $7,100 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Enbrel copay card. From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $2,355 per month-equivalent — a two-thirds cut. Etanercept biosimilars are also available and cheaper.

## Otezla (apremilast)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/otezla-cost/
Class: PDE4 inhibitor (oral)
Short answer: Otezla costs about $4,200 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Otezla copay card. Otezla is in the second Medicare negotiation cycle, with a negotiated price effective 2027; until then Medicare patients rely on the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Tremfya (guselkumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/tremfya-cost/
Class: IL-23 inhibitor (subcutaneous, every 8 weeks)
Short answer: Tremfya's list price is about ~$13,000 per dose (every 8 weeks maintenance), but people with commercial insurance can pay as little as $0 per dose with Tremfya withMe. If you have Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but your total out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026. Uninsured or underinsured patients can apply to the Johnson & Johnson Patient Assistance Foundation (J&J withMe).

## Benlysta (belimumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/benlysta-cost/
Class: BLyS-specific inhibitor (weekly self-injection or IV)
Short answer: Benlysta's list price is ~$1,300/wk SC (about $5,200/mo), but people with commercial insurance may pay as little as $0 per prescription with the Benlysta Co-pay Program (an annual maximum applies). On Medicare Part D, the copay card can't be used, but total out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026. Uninsured or underinsured patients can apply for help through Together with GSK.

## Orencia (abatacept)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/orencia-cost/
Class: T-cell costimulation modulator (weekly self-injection or IV)
Short answer: Orencia has a list price of ~$5,000+/mo, and there is no biosimilar or generic yet. With commercial insurance, the Orencia On Call Co-pay Card can lower your cost to as little as $5 per month (not $0), with up to $15,000/yr in support. On Medicare, copay cards are not allowed, but Part D out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026, and the Bristol Myers Squibb Patient Assistance Foundation may help eligible patients.

## Olumiant (baricitinib)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/olumiant-cost/
Class: JAK inhibitor (oral, once daily)
Short answer: Olumiant has a list price of about ~$5,500/mo (4 mg). If you have commercial insurance, the Olumiant Savings Card can bring your cost to $5 per 30-day fill (not $0), with benefits worth up to $10,600/yr, 13 fills. On Medicare Part D, the card cannot be used, but your 2026 out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100, and the Lilly Cares Foundation may help if you qualify.

## Sotyktu (deucravacitinib)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/sotyktu-cost/
Class: TYK2 inhibitor (oral, once daily)
Short answer: Sotyktu has a list price of about ~$7,000/mo, but commercially insured patients can pay $0 per 30-day supply with the Sotyktu 360 Support Copay Program. Medicare Part D enrollees cannot use the copay card, but their out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Uninsured or underinsured patients can apply to the Bristol Myers Squibb Patient Assistance Foundation.

## Cyltezo (adalimumab-adbm)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/cyltezo-cost/
Class: Adalimumab (Humira) biosimilar — TNF inhibitor (subcutaneous)
Short answer: Cyltezo's list price is about ~$3,500 per 2-pen kit, which is below Humira's list price. With commercial insurance, you may pay as little as $0 per prescription through the CARECONNECT4ME Copay Program. On Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but your total out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Amjevita (adalimumab-atto)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/amjevita-cost/
Class: Adalimumab (Humira) biosimilar — TNF inhibitor (subcutaneous)
Short answer: Amjevita has a list price of ~$684 per 40 mg pen (biosimilar; varies). With commercial insurance, eligible patients may pay as little as $0 per monthly fill with Amjevita SupportPlus. On Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but your out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Simlandi (adalimumab-ryvk)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/simlandi-cost/
Class: Adalimumab (Humira) biosimilar — interchangeable TNF inhibitor (SC)
Short answer: Simlandi's list price is ~$551 per kit (biosimilar; below Humira). With commercial insurance, the Simlandi Savings Program can bring your cost to as little as $0 per prescription, subject to program terms. On Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but your annual out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Inflectra (infliximab-dyyb)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/inflectra-cost/
Class: Infliximab (Remicade) biosimilar — TNF inhibitor (IV infusion)
Short answer: Inflectra's list price is about ~$932 per 100 mg vial (biosimilar), and most infusions need more than one vial, plus facility and administration fees. With commercial insurance, the Inflectra Pfizer enCompass Co-Pay Program can bring your cost to as little as $0 per prescription, with a program maximum of $3,000–$12,000/yr. Medicare patients cannot use the co-pay card; because Inflectra is an infusion, it is usually billed under Medicare Part B, so the $2,100 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap generally does not apply to it.

## Kevzara (sarilumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/kevzara-cost/
Class: IL-6 receptor antagonist (self-injection)
Short answer: Kevzara has a list price of ~$2,094 per dose (every 2 weeks), so the cash cost is high. With commercial insurance, the KevzaraConnect Copay Card can bring your cost down to as little as $0 per month (up to $15,000/yr, 12 uses). On Medicare Part D, copay cards can't be used, but your annual out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Vtama (tapinarof)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/autoimmune/vtama-cost/
Class: Topical aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist (cream)
Short answer: Vtama has a list price of ~$1,556 per 60 g tube. People with commercial insurance may pay as little as $0 to $35 per prescription with the Vtama Savings Card (commercial), subject to program terms. On Medicare Part D, the savings card cannot be used, but out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Trulicity (dulaglutide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/trulicity-cost/
Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Trulicity costs about $990 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $25 a month with the Trulicity savings card (if their plan covers it). There is no generic. Medicare patients pay plan cost-share under the $2,100 Part D cap; the uninsured can apply to Lilly Cares.

## Rybelsus (semaglutide (oral))
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/rybelsus-cost/
Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Rybelsus costs about $1,000 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $10 a month with the Rybelsus savings card (if covered). There is no generic. As a semaglutide product it is in the second Medicare negotiation cycle, with a negotiated price effective 2027.

## Victoza (liraglutide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/victoza-cost/
Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Branded Victoza lists around $820 a month. A cheaper authorized generic liraglutide is available and is usually the better-value route. Commercially insured patients may also use the Victoza savings card; Medicare patients pay plan cost-share under the $2,100 cap; the uninsured can apply to NovoCare.

## Jardiance (empagliflozin)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/jardiance-cost/
Class: SGLT2 inhibitor
Short answer: Jardiance costs about $640 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $10 a month with the Jardiance savings card (up to $100 per 30-day or $450 per 90-day supply). From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $197 per 30-day supply — a cut of roughly two-thirds.

## Farxiga (dapagliflozin)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/farxiga-cost/
Class: SGLT2 inhibitor
Short answer: Farxiga costs about $600 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 a month with the Farxiga savings card. From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $178.50 per 30-day supply.

## Mounjaro (tirzepatide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/mounjaro-cost/
Class: GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Mounjaro costs about $1,080 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients with coverage can pay as little as $25 a month with the Mounjaro savings card; those whose commercial plan doesn't cover it may pay a capped amount instead. Mounjaro is in the second Medicare negotiation cycle, with a negotiated price effective 2027 — not yet in 2026.

## Januvia (sitagliptin)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/januvia-cost/
Class: DPP-4 inhibitor
Short answer: Branded Januvia costs about $620 a month at list price. From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $113 per 30-day supply. Generic sitagliptin is beginning to reach pharmacies and will be the cheapest route once widely stocked.

## Tresiba (insulin degludec)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/tresiba-cost/
Class: Long-acting (basal) insulin
Short answer: Without insurance, Tresiba varies by form; cash roughly $150–560/mo. With commercial insurance, the Novo Nordisk savings offer can bring it down to as little as $35 per 30-day supply, and on Medicare, the federal $35/month insulin cap applies to covered insulin, with total Part D out-of-pocket costs capped at $2,100 in 2026. A generic insulin degludec is also available and may cost less.

## Kerendia (finerenone)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/kerendia-cost/
Class: Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (oral, once daily)
Short answer: Kerendia has a list price of about ~$707/mo. With commercial insurance, the Kerendia Savings Card can bring the cost to as little as $0 per monthly prescription, with savings of up to $3,000/yr. On Medicare Part D, the card cannot be used, but your total out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026, and uninsured or underinsured patients can apply to the Bayer US Patient Assistance Foundation.

## Basaglar (insulin glargine)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/diabetes/basaglar-cost/
Class: Long-acting (basal) insulin (follow-on biologic)
Short answer: Basaglar's cash price is about ~$327 per 15 mL (cash), but most people with commercial insurance or no insurance can pay as little as $35 per 30-day supply with the Lilly Insulin Value Program (commercial or cash). On Medicare Part D, insulin is capped at $35 per month under federal law, and total 2026 Part D out-of-pocket spending is capped at $2,100. If you can't afford it, the Lilly Cares Foundation may help.

## Miebo (perfluorohexyloctane)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/eye-care/miebo-cost/
Class: Ophthalmic solution for dry eye (eye drop)
Short answer: Miebo has a list price of about ~$1,352 per bottle, but commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 per prescription with the Miebo Copay Card, and uninsured patients can pay about $225 through the same program. Medicare Part D patients cannot use the copay card, but their yearly out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Patients with limited income may also qualify for the Bausch + Lomb Patient Assistance Program.

## Eylea (aflibercept)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/eye-care/eylea-cost/
Class: Anti-VEGF injection (intravitreal)
Short answer: Eylea has a list price of ~$1,999 per injection, before the clinic's administration fees. With commercial insurance, the Eylea4U Commercial Copay Card can bring your cost down to as little as $0 per treatment, with assistance of up to $20,000/yr plus $1,000 administration. Medicare usually covers Eylea under Part B because it is given in the doctor's office, so the $2,100 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap generally does not apply. Medicare and Medicaid patients cannot use the copay card but may qualify for EYLEA4U Patient Assistance.

## Wegovy (semaglutide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/glp-1-weight-loss/wegovy-cost/
Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Wegovy costs about $1,350 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients with coverage can pay as little as $0 with the Wegovy savings card. For cash payers, NovoCare self-pay offers Wegovy well below list price. Medicare does not cover Wegovy for weight loss (it may cover it to reduce cardiovascular risk in specific patients).

## Zepbound (tirzepatide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/glp-1-weight-loss/zepbound-cost/
Class: GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Zepbound costs about $1,060 a month at list price for the pens, but self-pay single-dose vials through LillyDirect are cheaper. Commercially insured patients with coverage can pay as little as $25 with the Zepbound savings card. Medicare does not cover it for weight loss.

## Ozempic (semaglutide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/glp-1-weight-loss/ozempic-cost/
Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Ozempic costs about $970 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients with coverage can pay as little as $25 with the Ozempic savings card. Ozempic (semaglutide) is in the second Medicare negotiation cycle, with a negotiated price effective 2027. Medicare covers it for diabetes, not weight loss.

## Saxenda (liraglutide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/glp-1-weight-loss/saxenda-cost/
Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Short answer: Branded Saxenda costs about $1,350 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can use the Saxenda savings card, but the bigger story is generic liraglutide, which is emerging and much cheaper. Medicare does not cover it for weight loss.

## Contrave (naltrexone/bupropion)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/glp-1-weight-loss/contrave-cost/
Class: Combination weight-loss oral
Short answer: Contrave lists at about $700 a month, but the manufacturer's Contrave Now / cash program offers it far cheaper — often a fixed low monthly price regardless of insurance. That makes it one of the more affordable prescription weight-loss options.

## Brilinta (ticagrelor)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/brilinta-cost/
Class: P2Y12 antiplatelet
Short answer: Brand Brilinta lists around $550 a month, but generic ticagrelor is now available and is usually the cheapest route — often well under $100 a month with a discount card. Commercially insured patients may also use the Brilinta savings card; Medicare patients pay plan cost-share under the $2,100 cap.

## Eliquis (apixaban)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/eliquis-cost/
Class: Factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulant
Short answer: Eliquis costs about $600 a month (roughly $7,100 a year) at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $10 a month with the Eliquis Co-pay Card. From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $231 per 30-day supply, applied automatically at the pharmacy for Part D members.

## Xarelto (rivaroxaban)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/xarelto-cost/
Class: Factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulant
Short answer: Xarelto costs about $550 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Janssen CarePath copay card. From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $197 per 30-day supply, applied automatically for Part D members.

## Entresto (sacubitril/valsartan)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/entresto-cost/
Class: ARNI (angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor)
Short answer: Entresto costs about $600 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $10 a month with the Entresto copay card. From 1 January 2026 the Medicare-negotiated price is about $295 per 30-day supply, applied automatically for Part D members.

## Repatha (evolocumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/repatha-cost/
Class: PCSK9 inhibitor
Short answer: Repatha costs about $650 a month (roughly $7,800 a year) at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $5 a month with the Repatha copay card. Repatha does not currently have a Medicare-negotiated price, so Medicare patients pay their plan's cost-share up to the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Pradaxa (dabigatran)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/pradaxa-cost/
Class: Direct thrombin inhibitor anticoagulant
Short answer: Branded Pradaxa costs about $550 a month at list price, but generic dabigatran is available and much cheaper — often well under $100 a month with a discount card. Commercially insured patients can also use the Pradaxa savings card.

## Camzyos (mavacamten)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/heart-blood-thinners/camzyos-cost/
Class: Cardiac myosin inhibitor (oral) — REMS program
Short answer: Camzyos has a list price of about ~$8,537/mo before insurance. With commercial insurance, the Camzyos Co-pay Program can lower your cost to $10 per monthly prescription (not $0), subject to monthly and annual limits. On Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but your 2026 out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 for the year.

## Descovy (emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/descovy-cost/
Class: HIV NRTI backbone / PrEP
Short answer: Descovy lists around $2,200 a month. But if you take it for PrEP, the ACA requires most commercial plans to cover PrEP and its associated visits at $0, so you often pay nothing. Commercially insured patients can also use the Gilead Advancing Access copay card ($0); uninsured patients have Ready, Set, PrEP and ADAP. There is no generic Descovy (though generic F/TDF exists for PrEP).

## Dovato (dolutegravir/lamivudine)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/dovato-cost/
Class: HIV two-drug single-tablet regimen
Short answer: Dovato costs about $3,100 a month at list price, but almost no one pays that. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the ViiVConnect copay card; uninsured patients use ADAP or ViiV patient assistance; Medicare patients pay plan cost-share under the $2,100 Part D cap. There is no generic.

## Genvoya (elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/genvoya-cost/
Class: HIV single-tablet regimen
Short answer: Genvoya costs about $3,900 a month at list price, but almost no one pays that. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Gilead Advancing Access card; uninsured patients use ADAP or Gilead assistance; Medicare patients pay plan cost-share under the $2,100 Part D cap. There is no generic.

## Biktarvy (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/biktarvy-cost/
Class: HIV integrase inhibitor single-tablet regimen
Short answer: Biktarvy costs about $4,000 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 with the Biktarvy copay card. Uninsured and low-income patients can access it through Gilead Advancing Access, Ryan White or state ADAP. Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Epclusa (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/epclusa-cost/
Class: Hepatitis C direct-acting antiviral
Short answer: Branded Epclusa lists around $25,000 for a 12-week course, but an authorized generic (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir) is available at a fraction of that — often a few hundred to a couple of thousand dollars for the full course. Commercially insured patients can use the copay card; assistance programs help others.

## Mavyret (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/mavyret-cost/
Class: Hepatitis C direct-acting antiviral
Short answer: Mavyret lists around $13,000 for an 8-week course at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $5 with the Mavyret copay card. Uninsured, income-eligible patients can get it free through AbbVie; Medicare patients are protected by the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Vemlidy (tenofovir alafenamide)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/vemlidy-cost/
Class: Nucleotide analogue for chronic hepatitis B (once daily)
Short answer: Vemlidy has a list price of about ~$1,587/mo. With commercial insurance, the Vemlidy Support Path Copay Coupon can bring your cost to as little as $0 per prescription (up to $6,000/yr, no monthly limit). On Medicare Part D, the coupon can't be used, but your yearly out-of-pocket drug spending is capped at $2,100 in 2026, and Gilead Support Path may help if you are uninsured or underinsured.

## Isentress (raltegravir)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/isentress-cost/
Class: HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor
Short answer: Isentress has a list price of about ~$2,090/mo (400 mg), but most commercially insured patients pay far less. With the Isentress Savings Coupon, eligible patients may pay as little as $0 per prescription, with the program covering up to $6,800 total. Medicare Part D enrollees can't use the coupon, but their out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

## Cabenuva (cabotegravir/rilpivirine)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/hiv-hepatitis/cabenuva-cost/
Class: Long-acting injectable HIV-1 regimen (monthly or every 2 months)
Short answer: Cabenuva's list price is about ~$4,769–7,150 per injection set, but commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 per prescription with the ViiV Connect Savings Program (up to $13,000/yr plus $100/treatment administration). If Cabenuva is covered under your Medicare Part D plan, your 2026 out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100, and uninsured or underinsured patients can apply to ViiV Connect for assistance.

## Veozah (fezolinetant)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/menopause-womens-health/veozah-cost/
Class: NK3 receptor antagonist (oral) for menopausal hot flashes
Short answer: Veozah has a list price of about ~$578/mo. People with commercial insurance can use the Veozah Savings Card to pay $0 for the first month, then $30 per monthly refill, with a program maximum of up to $4,000/yr. The card cannot be used with Medicare or Medicaid, but Medicare Part D out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

Class: GnRH antagonist combination (oral)
Short answer: Myfembree has a list price of about ~$1,302/mo, and there is no generic or biosimilar. On Medicare Part D, the copay card can't be used, but your total out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

URL: https://rxcostguide.com/menopause-womens-health/tymlos-cost/
Class: Parathyroid hormone-related protein analog (self-injection)
Short answer: Tymlos has a list price of about ~$2,935/mo, but commercially insured patients may pay as little as $0 per month with the Tymlos Savings Card, subject to a limit of 12 fills/yr and an annual cap. On Medicare Part D, the copay card cannot be used, but 2026 out-of-pocket drug costs are capped at $2,100 for the year. ## Vraylar (cariprazine)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/mental-health/vraylar-cost/
Class: Atypical antipsychotic
Short answer: Vraylar costs about $1,550 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can pay as little as $0 a month with the Vraylar Savings Card. There is no generic yet. Vraylar is in the second Medicare negotiation cycle, with a negotiated price effective 1 January 2027 — until then Medicare patients pay their plan cost-share under the $2,100 Part D cap.

## Latuda (lurasidone)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/mental-health/latuda-cost/
Class: Atypical antipsychotic
Short answer: Branded Latuda lists around $1,600 a month, but generic lurasidone is far cheaper — often $30–$60 a month with a discount card — and is the single biggest reason this hub exists. Generic lurasidone is usually the cheapest second-generation antipsychotic, so it is worth asking your prescriber and pharmacist about it first.

## Trintellix (vortioxetine)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/mental-health/trintellix-cost/
Class: Antidepressant (serotonin modulator)
Short answer: Trintellix costs about $570 a month at list price. Commercially insured patients can usually pay as little as $10 a month with the Trintellix savings card. There is no generic yet. Because many cheap generic antidepressants exist, it is worth asking whether one suits you before paying brand prices.

## Ocrevus (ocrelizumab)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/multiple-sclerosis/ocrevus-cost/
Class: CD20 monoclonal antibody (IV infusion every 6 months)
Short answer: Ocrevus has a list price of ~$21,000 per infusion (about $42,000/yr), before infusion-center charges. With commercial insurance, you may pay as little as $0 per infusion with the Ocrevus Co-Pay Program, which covers up to $20,000/yr for drug plus infusion support. On Medicare, the copay card cannot be used, and because Ocrevus is a clinic-administered infusion it is usually billed under Part B rather than Part D, so the $2,100 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap often does not apply; the Genentech Patient Foundation may help eligible patients who are uninsured or underinsured.

## Kesimpta (ofatumumab)

## Uplizna (inebilizumab-cdon)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/multiple-sclerosis/uplizna-cost/
Class: CD19 monoclonal antibody (IV infusion every 6 months)

Because Uplizna is infused in a clinic, it is usually billed under Part B rather than Part D, so the $2,100 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap applies only if your plan covers it under Part D. Patient assistance through Amgen By Your Side / Good Days may help if you qualify.

## Lupron Depot (leuprolide acetate)
URL: https://rxcostguide.com/oncology/lupron-cost/
Class: GnRH agonist (injectable depot)
Short answer: Lupron Depot's list price is about ~$1,855–13,216 per injection (dosing-interval dependent). With commercial insurance, you may pay as little as $10 per dose for endometriosis with the Lupron Depot Savings Card (commercial). Medicare patients cannot use the card. Because Lupron Depot is given in a clinic, Medicare usually covers it under Part B, so the $2,100 2026 Part D out-of-pocket cap often does not apply. Patients without adequate coverage can apply to myAbbVie Assist.
